newsitem.title: USA: U.S. drops proposal to simplify natgas royalties.
newsitem.headline: U.S. drops proposal to simplify natgas royalties.

text.p: The U.S. Minerals Management Service said Tuesday it was dropping a plan to change the way it calculated natural gas royalties because under the new method it would have collected less money.

"After consideration of several pertinent factors, including ... the results of an internal cost-benefit analysis, which indicated a potential $20 million or more annual revenue loss from the proposed rule, we have decided it is best not to amend the existing regulations at this time," said MMS director Cynthia Quarterman.
The agency collects about $2 billion a year in natural gas royalties from production on federal leases onshore and offshore.

The proposal, issued in late 1995 after two years of talks with state and industry officials, called for royalties from gas produced on federal land mainly to be based on published price indexes instead of on producers' gross proceeds.
The new method was meant to reflect changes in the deregulated natural gas market and streamline royalty payments without affecting the amount of money the agency collected.
Natural gas industry officials said they were angry that MMS decided to drop the proposed rule, which they had expected to go into effect this summer.

"Obviously we are disappointed," said Nicholas Bush, president of the Natural Gas Supply Association. "The producing industry has expended hundreds of thousands of dollars and considerable time -- more than two years -- in an effort to modify gas valuation so that it is simpler to administer and more equitable to all parties."

The agency's royalty valuation chief, Debbie Gibbs Tschudy, said MMS was still looking for ways to improve the system, adding that it had decided to drop its proposal partly because the market was still rapidly changing.

Tschudy said MMS had not done a cost-benefit analysis on its proposal earlier, because it only recently obtained enough data reflecting natural gas market activity under the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission's landmark 1992 Order 636, which altered the way natural gas was traded.
MMS asked the industry for comment on two new options for royalty calculations, but it set no deadline for receiving public input.
The first option was based on an index price but linked to gross proceeds earned by producers who wanted to pay based on an index price.
The second option called for creating a panel that would set the price on which to base royalties.
"We have not had time to review the new proposed options," Bush said. "We are eager to discuss them with MMS and provide comments as soon as possible."
